questions.q: On what date in 1950 did North Korean forces cross the 38th parallel to invade South Korea?
questions.explain: North Korea attacked across the 38th parallel on June 25, 1950, with about 90,000 soldiers in eight divisions and an armored brigade.

questions.q: Which body condemned the North Korean attack on June 25, 1950, and called for a cease-fire and withdrawal to the 38th parallel?
questions.explain: On the day of the attack the UN Security Council condemned North Korea and called for a cease-fire and a pullback to the 38th parallel.

questions.q: Who commanded Far East Command in Tokyo when the Korean War broke out in June 1950?
questions.explain: Truman ordered MacArthur, commander of Far East Command, to evacuate American dependents and send ammunition to South Korea on June 25, 1950.

questions.q: What was the approximate size of the South Korean army when North Korea invaded, according to the U.S. Army history?
questions.explain: The U.S. Army history lists about 98,000 South Korean soldiers and no tanks against roughly 90,000 North Koreans backed by armor.

questions.q: About how many American advisers made up the U.S. Korean Military Advisory Group, the only American support present when the war began?
questions.explain: The U.S. Korean Military Advisory Group of about 500 men was the only American military support in place when the invasion began.

questions.q: What was Task Force Smith, the first American ground unit to fight in Korea near Osan in July 1950?
options: A Marine brigade of about 5,000 men from Okinawa
An airborne regiment dropped behind North Korean lines
A force of about 540 men from the 24th Infantry Division
A British infantry brigade of about 2,000 men
questions.explain: Task Force Smith, about 540 men of the 24th Infantry Division, lost more than 150 men killed, wounded or captured near Osan and left behind much of its equipment.

questions.q: What was the Pusan Perimeter, established in early August 1950?
options: A fortified wall along the Yalu River
A naval blockade of the North Korean coast
A buffer zone created by the armistice
A defensive line of about 140 miles in southeastern Korea
questions.explain: UN forces held the Pusan Perimeter, a roughly 140-mile defensive line, until the Inchon landing and breakout in September.

questions.q: Which Army division formed part of the Inchon force alongside the 1st Marine Division?
questions.explain: The Inchon force included the 1st Marine Division and the Army's 7th Infantry Division, under MacArthur's overall command.

questions.q: What name was given to the Inchon operation planned by General MacArthur?
questions.explain: Operation Chromite was the code name of the September 1950 Inchon landing, which captured Wolmi-do quickly before the main landing.

questions.q: What natural feature made Inchon a difficult landing site that the planners had to overcome?
options: Extreme tides, fast currents and tall seawalls
Dense jungle and swamps behind the landing beaches
Thick coral reefs that blocked landing craft
Constant fog that grounded all aircraft
questions.explain: Inchon had extreme tides, narrow channels, fast currents and seawalls, so the landing had to be timed to a very short window.

questions.q: Which island fell to Marines at Inchon by about noon on September 15, 1950, before the main landings on Red and Blue Beaches?
questions.explain: Wolmi-do was captured by about noon, and Marines then landed on Red and Blue Beaches later that day at high tide.

questions.q: On which Pacific island did President Truman meet General MacArthur in October 1950 to discuss the war?
questions.explain: Truman and MacArthur met on Wake Island on October 15, 1950, after UN forces had pushed the North Koreans back north of the 38th parallel.

questions.q: What did Marine Maj. Gen. Oliver P. Smith say when his troops fought out of the Chosin Reservoir encirclement?
options: "Nuts! We will hold this frozen ground until relieved."
"I shall return to this reservoir with a larger force."
"We have met the enemy, and he is ours, in this valley."
Retreat, hell! We're just attacking in another direction.
questions.explain: Smith's remark, often misquoted as "advancing in a different direction," became famous. The breakout from Chosin ended at the Hungnam perimeter by December 11, 1950.

questions.q: Which North Korean port was the site of a large seaborne evacuation of U.N. forces that ended around December 24, 1950?
questions.explain: X Corps fought a running battle to the coast and finished evacuating from Hungnam on December 24, 1950.

questions.q: Which general took command of the Eighth Army in Korea after Walton Walker died in a December 1950 accident?
questions.explain: Lt. Gen. Matthew Ridgway arrived on December 26, 1950, three days after Walker's death, and began a counteroffensive in January 1951.

questions.q: On April 11, 1951, President Truman relieved MacArthur and named which general to replace him?
questions.explain: Truman relieved MacArthur on April 11, 1951, and Ridgway took over as commander of the United Nations forces.

questions.q: What principle did Truman defend when he dismissed General MacArthur in April 1951?
options: The need to expand the war into China
The right of generals to set foreign policy
The authority of the Senate over troop commanders
questions.explain: Truman argued that a general had to accept the policies set by the elected commander in chief, even if he disagreed with them.

questions.q: Where did armistice negotiations to end the Korean War begin in July 1951?
questions.explain: Korean War armistice talks began at Kaesong on July 10, 1951. They later moved to Panmunjom, where the armistice was signed in July 1953.

questions.q: What did the two sides agree in November 1951 about the line separating their forces?
options: The Yalu River would mark the new border
The 38th parallel would be restored at once
Seoul would become a neutral city
The existing line of contact would be the demarcation line if a deal came in 30 days
questions.explain: On November 27, 1951, negotiators agreed to use the existing line of contact as the demarcation line, provided an armistice was signed within 30 days.

questions.q: On what date was the Korean War armistice signed?
questions.explain: The armistice signed on July 27, 1953, stopped all fighting after about 37 months of combat.

questions.q: About how long did combat last in the Korean War, according to the U.S. Army history?
questions.explain: Combat in Korea lasted 37 months, from June 1950 to July 1953.

questions.q: What kind of agreement ended the fighting in Korea in 1953?
options: A military armistice, not a peace treaty
A treaty ratified by the U.S. Senate
A formal alliance between North and South Korea
A United Nations trusteeship over the peninsula
questions.explain: The armistice is a ceasefire between military commands. No final peace treaty has ever been signed, so the war has not formally ended.

questions.q: Which Korean leader refused to sign the 1953 armistice because he rejected the outcome?
options: Kim Il Sung of North Korea
Park Chung Hee of South Korea
questions.explain: South Korea did not sign the armistice because President Syngman Rhee wanted the war to continue until the peninsula was reunified.

questions.q: Which pair of U.N. Command officers signed the armistice at Panmunjom for the United Nations side?
options: Matthew Ridgway and James Van Fleet
William K. Harrison Jr. and Mark W. Clark
questions.explain: Harrison signed at Panmunjom and Clark, the U.N. commander, signed afterward. Nam Il, Kim Il Sung and Peng Dehuai signed for the other side.

questions.q: About how wide is the Demilitarized Zone created by the 1953 Korean armistice?
questions.explain: The DMZ is a buffer of about four kilometers following the line where the armies stood when the armistice was signed.

questions.q: Which group of countries made up the Neutral Nations Supervisory Commission set up by the 1953 Korean armistice?
options: Japan, Australia, Thailand and the Philippines
questions.explain: The commission was created by the armistice to help supervise its terms.

questions.q: Who was the commander of the U.N. Command when the Korean armistice was signed in July 1953?
questions.explain: Clark replaced Ridgway in May 1952 and commanded the United Nations Command through the July 1953 armistice.

questions.q: Which U.S. Army general succeeded Ridgway as Eighth Army commander on April 14, 1951?
questions.explain: Lt. Gen. James Van Fleet took command of the Eighth Army on April 14, 1951, when Ridgway moved up to replace MacArthur.

questions.q: Which lieutenant general replaced Van Fleet as Eighth Army commander in February 1953?
questions.explain: Lt. Gen. Maxwell Taylor took command of the Eighth Army in February 1953 and commanded it at the end of the war.

questions.q: How many of the 131 Medals of Honor awarded to servicemembers in Korea went to Army soldiers, according to the U.S. Army?
questions.explain: U.S. Army personnel received 78 of the 131 Medals of Honor awarded to servicemembers who served in the Korean War.

questions.q: Which was NOT among the Army divisions sent to Korea?
questions.explain: The Army sent eight divisions, among them the 1st Cavalry and the 2nd, 3rd, 7th, 24th, 25th, 40th and 45th Infantry Divisions.

questions.q: Which Soviet move in June 1951 opened a diplomatic path toward ceasefire talks in Korea?
options: The Soviets withdrew from the UN permanently
The Soviet delegate to the UN proposed a cease-fire
Stalin invited Truman to a Moscow summit
China offered to leave the Yalu River unguarded
questions.explain: On June 23, 1951, the Soviet Union's UN delegate proposed a ceasefire, which led to the talks that began in July at Kaesong.

questions.q: How many statues stand in the "Column" of servicemen at the Korean War Veterans Memorial?
questions.explain: Frank Gaylord sculpted 19 stainless steel figures of a patrol moving through rugged ground. Their reflections in the wall make 38.

questions.q: Who sculpted the nineteen servicemen statues at the Korean War Veterans Memorial?
questions.explain: Frank Gaylord created the 19 sculptures of a patrol. Frederick Hart and Glenna Goodacre made figures at the Vietnam memorials.

questions.q: What material are the 19 patrol statues at the Korean War Veterans Memorial made from?
questions.explain: The 19 figures are stainless steel, each about seven and a half feet tall, arranged as a patrol advancing toward an American flag.

questions.q: How many of the 19 patrol statues represent each service: the breakdown at the Korean War Veterans Memorial?
options: 10 Army, 5 Marine, 2 Navy and 2 Air Force
12 Army, 4 Marine, 2 Navy and 1 Air Force
14 Army, 3 Marine, 1 Navy and 1 Air Force
questions.explain: The patrol includes 14 Army, 3 Marine Corps, 1 Navy corpsman and 1 Air Force forward air observer, representing the four services.

questions.q: What does the long black granite Mural Wall at the Korean War Veterans Memorial show?
options: The names of every American who died in the war
Faces of service members sandblasted into the granite
A map of the battles of the war
The text of the armistice agreement
questions.explain: The Mural Wall carries more than 2,000 photographic images of Korean War service members, and it reflects the statues.

questions.q: Who created the Mural Wall of etched images at the Korean War Veterans Memorial?
questions.explain: Artist Louis Nelson designed the Mural Wall, whose images were sandblasted into black granite from California.

questions.q: The Korean War Veterans Memorial's 19 statues are reflected in the polished Mural Wall. How many figures do the statues and their reflections make together?
questions.explain: The 19 statues and their 19 reflections make 38, a number the National Park Service links to the 38th parallel.

questions.q: What does the United Nations Wall at the Korean War Veterans Memorial honor?
options: The founding of the United Nations in 1945
American prisoners of war held in North Korea
Korean civilians who died in the war
The countries that fought with the United States in Korea
questions.explain: The U.N. Wall lists 21 other countries that fought alongside the United States, a reminder that Korea was a coalition effort.

questions.q: Which flowering plant, South Korea's national flower, is planted at the Korean War Veterans Memorial?
questions.explain: Rose of Sharon bushes, the national flower of South Korea, are planted at the memorial.

questions.q: When was the Korean War Veterans Memorial dedicated?
questions.explain: The memorial was dedicated on July 27, 1995, the 42nd anniversary of the armistice, by President Clinton and South Korean President Kim Young Sam.

questions.q: Which president led the groundbreaking for the Korean War Veterans Memorial on June 14, 1992?
questions.explain: George H. W. Bush led the groundbreaking in 1992. President Clinton dedicated the finished memorial three years later.

questions.q: Which architecture firm produced the final design of the Korean War Veterans Memorial after a Penn State team withdrew?
questions.explain: A Penn State team won the 1986 design competition but withdrew after required changes. Cooper-Lecky Architects then led the final design.

questions.q: On the Mall, where does the Korean War Veterans Memorial stand?
options: In West Potomac Park, south of the Reflecting Pool
In front of the Capitol west steps
In Constitution Gardens, near the Vietnam Memorial wall
questions.explain: The memorial lies in West Potomac Park, south of the Reflecting Pool and southeast of the Lincoln Memorial.

questions.q: What was added to the Korean War Veterans Memorial and dedicated on July 27, 2022?
options: The Wall of Remembrance listing the names of the dead
questions.explain: The Wall of Remembrance, dedicated on the 69th anniversary of the armistice, lists the U.S. and KATUSA service members killed in Korea.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation KATUSA, used on the Korean War Veterans Memorial's Wall of Remembrance, stand for?
options: Korean Army Training Unit South Asia
Korean Army Tactical Unit of the Seventh Army
Korean Augmentation to the United States Army
questions.explain: The wall lists more than 7,000 KATUSA soldiers, South Koreans who served with U.S. Army units, alongside the Americans killed in the war.

questions.q: About how many Americans killed in Korea does the Korean War Veterans Memorial's Wall of Remembrance name?
questions.explain: The National Park Service says the wall lists the names of more than 36,000 Americans killed in the Korean War.

questions.q: The 2010 Federal Circuit ruling in a copyright suit concerned which use of the Korean War Veterans Memorial's statues?
options: A television advertisement for a veterans charity group
A replica displayed in a shopping mall
A postage stamp using a photograph of the sculpture
A commemorative coin from the U.S. Mint
questions.explain: The court found sculptor Frank Gaylord was owed compensation for a stamp using a photograph of his work.

questions.q: Which law, passed in 1986, authorized the Korean War Veterans Memorial?
questions.explain: Public Law 99-572 authorized the memorial on federal land in the national capital area.

questions.q: How many other nations does the U.N. Wall at the Korean War Veterans Memorial list besides the United States?
questions.explain: The National Park Service says the U.N. Wall lists 22 countries including the United States, so 21 others sent combat troops or medical support.

questions.q: Which Viet Minh general commanded the forces that won at Dien Bien Phu in 1954?
questions.explain: Giap surrounded the French base and placed heavy artillery on hills overlooking the valley, forcing the garrison to surrender.

questions.q: At what line did the 1954 Geneva Accords temporarily divide Vietnam?
questions.explain: Vietnam was split at the 17th parallel, with Ho Chi Minh governing the North. Reunification elections planned for 1956 were never held.

questions.q: How did the Senate vote on the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution on August 7, 1964?
questions.explain: The Senate approved the resolution 88-2, with Wayne Morse and Ernest Gruening opposed. The House had already passed it unanimously.

questions.q: Which Senate committee chairman steered the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution through the Senate at President Johnson's request?
questions.explain: Fulbright chaired the Foreign Relations Committee and managed the resolution on the Senate floor. By 1966 his committee held televised hearings on the war.

questions.q: What did Capt. John Herrick, the destroyer division commander aboard the Maddox, cable on August 4, 1964, that the administration did not share with Congress?
options: Proof that North Vietnam had sunk the ship
A plan to attack Hanoi directly
Doubts about whether a second attack had really occurred
questions.explain: The commander questioned whether the August 4 attack happened, but the administration announced retaliatory strikes without telling Congress of these doubts.

questions.q: Which presidential candidate did Lyndon Johnson defeat in the November 1964 election, a few months after the Tonkin Gulf Resolution?
questions.explain: Johnson beat Goldwater in November 1964 and expanded the war in early 1965, using the resolution as legal authority.

questions.q: About how many U.S. combat troops were in South Vietnam by the end of 1965?
questions.explain: After the Tonkin Gulf Resolution Johnson sent combat forces. U.S. troops there numbered over 150,000 by the end of 1965 and over 530,000 by 1968.

questions.q: When did Operation Rolling Thunder begin?
questions.explain: The bombing campaign began on March 2, 1965, after reprisal raids called Flaming Dart in February following attacks on U.S. installations.

questions.q: Which attack on a U.S. airfield on February 7, 1965, prompted the reprisal raid Operation Flaming Dart?
options: The attack on the U.S. embassy in Saigon
questions.explain: Operation Flaming Dart followed the attack on Camp Holloway, and a second reprisal followed an attack at Qui Nhon, as Rolling Thunder was prepared.

questions.q: What was one stated goal of Rolling Thunder?
options: To capture the North Vietnamese capital
To force France back into the war
To destroy the Chinese air force
To stop North Vietnam sending troops and supplies south
questions.explain: The campaign aimed to raise South Vietnamese morale, cut the flow of men and materiel south, and destroy North Vietnam's transport and industry.

questions.q: What does "Tet" refer to in the name of the Tet Offensive?
options: The Vietnamese Lunar New Year holiday
A mountain range in the central highlands of Vietnam
A major river in the south
questions.explain: Tet is short for Tet Nguyen Dan, the Lunar New Year. Many South Vietnamese soldiers were on holiday leave when the attacks began.

questions.q: Which city saw about a month of fighting during the Tet Offensive that destroyed much of it?
questions.explain: Fighting in Hue lasted about a month and destroyed much of the city.

questions.q: Hanoi expected the Tet Offensive to trigger what?
options: A coup against Ho Chi Minh
A popular uprising against the South Vietnamese government
A Chinese invasion of the South
questions.explain: Planners expected a general uprising to topple the Saigon government. It never happened, and the offensive was a military defeat for the North.

questions.q: Why was the Tet Offensive a political turning point in the United States?
options: It showed that the draft was no longer needed
It proved the South Vietnamese army had won the war
It shocked Americans who had been told the enemy was being defeated
It ended all fighting for a year
questions.explain: Although the offensive failed militarily, it contradicted optimistic official claims, and public support for the war declined.

questions.q: How many of South Vietnam's 44 provincial capitals were attacked in the Tet Offensive?
questions.explain: Communist forces attacked 36 of the 44 provincial capitals and Saigon itself, striking more than 100 towns and cities in all.

questions.q: Which U.S. base saw a siege that continued for two months after the main Tet attacks?
questions.explain: Fighting around the Khe Sanh base continued for about two more months after the main attacks of January 1968.

questions.q: On what date in 1968 did U.S. soldiers kill hundreds of unarmed civilians at My Lai?
questions.explain: On March 16, 1968, soldiers of Charlie Company killed hundreds of civilians in Son My village. The Army counted 347, and Vietnam lists 504.

questions.q: Which Army officer was the only man convicted of crimes in the My Lai massacre?
questions.explain: Calley was convicted in 1971 of the premeditated murder of at least 22 villagers and sentenced to life. His sentence was reduced on review and he was freed in 1974.

questions.q: Which helicopter pilot tried to stop the killing at My Lai and reported it to his superiors?
questions.explain: Warrant Officer Thompson landed to protect civilians. Ron Ridenhour, who was not present, later wrote to Congress and Army leaders seeking an investigation.

questions.q: Which journalist broke the story of the My Lai massacre in November 1969?
questions.explain: Hersh's reporting in November 1969 caused public outrage. The Army then named General William Peers to investigate the incident and the cover-up.

questions.q: What was the official U.S. Army report on the My Lai massacre and its cover-up, issued in 1970, known as?
questions.explain: Lt. Gen. William Peers was appointed in November 1969. His inquiry, completed in March 1970, criticized the soldiers and officers involved and the cover-up.

questions.q: Who ordered the secret study that became known as the Pentagon Papers?
questions.explain: McNamara created the Vietnam Study Task Force on June 17, 1967. Its report traced U.S. involvement in Vietnam from 1945 through the Johnson years.

questions.q: By what vote did the Supreme Court decide New York Times Co. v. United States, the Pentagon Papers case?
questions.explain: The justices wrote nine separate opinions in the decision of June 30, 1971, which refused to allow prior restraint of the newspapers.

questions.q: Which two newspapers published excerpts of the Pentagon Papers in June 1971?
options: The Chicago Tribune and The Los Angeles Times
The New York Times and The Washington Post
The Wall Street Journal and USA Today
The Boston Globe and The Baltimore Sun
questions.explain: The Times began on June 13, 1971, and The Washington Post began its own series on June 18 after Ellsberg gave it portions.

questions.q: How many volumes did the Pentagon Papers study contain?
questions.explain: The study ran to 47 volumes, with about 3,000 pages of analysis and 4,000 pages of original documents.

questions.q: What was the policy of Vietnamization announced by President Nixon?
options: Dividing Vietnam into two permanent states
Training South Vietnamese forces to fight while U.S. ground troops withdrew
Handing the war to the United Nations
questions.explain: Vietnamization expanded and equipped the South Vietnamese army so it could take a larger combat role while U.S. ground troops came home.

questions.q: About how many students did the May 1970 Kent State shootings wound?
questions.explain: Four students were killed and nine wounded. One of the wounded, Dean Kahler, was permanently paralyzed.

questions.q: Two people were killed when police fired on a dormitory at which college in Mississippi in May 1970?
questions.explain: City police and state highway patrolmen fired on a women's dormitory at Jackson State just after midnight on May 15, 1970, eleven days after Kent State, killing two students.

questions.q: What did the President's Commission on Campus Unrest conclude about the Kent State shootings?
options: They were fully justified by an armed attack
They were caused by outside agitators alone
They were an accident with no one at fault
They were unnecessary, unwarranted and inexcusable
questions.explain: The commission also reported that the guardsmen's gunfire was not warranted by the danger they faced.

questions.q: Which two men negotiated the main terms of the Paris Peace Accords and shared the 1973 Nobel Peace Prize?
options: William Rogers and Pham Van Dong
Henry Kissinger and Le Duc Tho
Richard Nixon and Ho Chi Minh
Melvin Laird and Nguyen Van Thieu
questions.explain: Kissinger and Le Duc Tho were jointly awarded the 1973 Nobel Peace Prize. Le Duc Tho refused to accept it.

questions.q: Within how many days did the Paris Peace Accords require U.S. and allied forces to withdraw from Vietnam?
questions.explain: The agreement set a sixty-day deadline for withdrawal. American prisoners were returned mainly through Operation Homecoming.

questions.q: Which countries made up the International Commission of Control and Supervision created by the Paris accords?
questions.explain: The ICCS replaced the earlier commission to monitor the agreement. Its four members were originally Canada, Poland, Hungary and Indonesia.

questions.q: Which 1973 law, passed over President Nixon's veto, restricted the president's power to commit U.S. forces abroad?
questions.explain: Congress passed the War Powers Act in 1973 over Nixon's veto, after Congress had repealed the Tonkin Gulf Resolution in 1971.

questions.q: On what date did Saigon fall to North Vietnamese forces?
questions.explain: Saigon fell on April 30, 1975, ending South Vietnam's existence. Forces raised the Viet Cong flag over the Presidential Palace.

questions.q: What was Operation Frequent Wind?
options: The helicopter evacuation of Americans and South Vietnamese from Saigon
The airlift of supplies to Berlin
questions.explain: Operation Frequent Wind was called the largest helicopter evacuation in history, flying about 7,000 people out of Saigon.

questions.q: Which general became South Vietnam's president for a day or two and surrendered to the communists in April 1975?
questions.explain: Minh replaced Tran Van Huong as president on April 28, 1975, and surrendered two days later, on April 30, as the regime collapsed.

questions.q: North Vietnam renamed its final offensive on April 14, 1975, in honor of whom?
questions.explain: The Politburo named the final push the Ho Chi Minh Campaign in April 1975. It ended with the fall of Saigon on April 30.

questions.q: Which president announced Operation Babylift on April 3, 1975, to evacuate children from Vietnam?
questions.explain: Ford announced Operation Babylift on April 3, 1975, and approved evacuation plans as Saigon fell weeks later.

questions.q: How old was Maya Lin when her design for the Vietnam Veterans Memorial was chosen?
questions.explain: Lin was a 21-year-old Yale architecture undergraduate when judges unanimously chose her entry from the competition.

questions.q: About how many designs were submitted to the Vietnam Veterans Memorial competition?
questions.explain: The Memorial Fund received 1,421 designs by the March 1981 deadline, and Lin's entry, number 1026, won.

questions.q: What did the Vietnam Veterans Memorial Fund use to pay for the memorial?
options: Private donations of more than $8 million
A bond issue by the National Park Service
questions.explain: The memorial was paid for with private contributions. Congress authorized the site, but the Fund raised more than $8 million from private donors.

questions.q: Which Vietnam veteran, inspired after seeing the film The Deer Hunter, founded the effort to build the Vietnam Veterans Memorial?
questions.explain: Scruggs wanted a tangible symbol of recognition for fellow soldiers. The Memorial Fund was formed by 1979.

questions.q: Which two Mall landmarks do the arms of the Vietnam Veterans Memorial wall point to?
options: The Capitol and the Jefferson Memorial
The White House and the Pentagon
The Korean War memorial and the World War II memorial
The Lincoln Memorial and the Washington Monument
questions.explain: One arm points toward the Lincoln Memorial and the other toward the Washington Monument, tying the wall to the Mall.

questions.q: How are the names ordered on the Vietnam Veterans Memorial?
options: By date of casualty, starting and ending at the center
questions.explain: Per the memorial fund, names run by date of casualty from the apex, beginning under 1959 on the east side, then resume on the west and end under 1975 at the apex.

questions.q: What symbol marks a service member listed as missing in action on the Vietnam Veterans Memorial?
questions.explain: A diamond marks those confirmed dead and a cross marks those missing. A circle is added around the cross if a missing person returns alive.

questions.q: How many military women are named among the dead on the Vietnam Veterans Memorial?
questions.explain: The names of eight military women who died in the war are inscribed on the Wall.

questions.q: How long did the reading of all the names engraved on the Wall take at Washington National Cathedral during the dedication week?
questions.explain: The National Cathedral hosted a 56-hour reading of all the engraved names as part of the dedication in 1982.

questions.q: Where was the black granite for 144 panels of the Vietnam Veterans Memorial quarried?
questions.explain: The granite came from India, was cut in Barre, Vermont, and was inscribed with names in Memphis, Tennessee.

questions.q: In which U.S. city were the names for the Vietnam Veterans Memorial inscribed on the panels?
questions.explain: Panels were cut in Barre, Vermont, and the names were inscribed in Memphis, Tennessee.

questions.q: Why was the Vietnam Veterans Memorial design controversial when it was unveiled?
options: Critics said a plain black wall lacked heroic imagery
It was built in a city outside Washington
It honored only officers and not enlisted men
It listed only the names of survivors
questions.explain: Some veterans and officials wanted traditional heroic statues. Critic Tom Carhart called the wall a black gash, and Interior Secretary James Watt delayed the building permit.

questions.q: Which sculptor created The Three Servicemen statue near the Vietnam Veterans Memorial?
questions.explain: Hart's bronze figures, in jungle gear, gaze toward the Wall. He said the work spoke of the bonds of love and sacrifice among men at war.

questions.q: When was The Three Servicemen statue dedicated at the Vietnam Veterans Memorial?
questions.explain: Frederick Hart's statue was added in 1984, two years after the Wall was dedicated.

questions.q: Which sculptor created the Vietnam Women's Memorial?
questions.explain: Goodacre's sculpture shows three nurses with a wounded soldier and honors the women who served in the Vietnam War.

questions.q: What does the Vietnam Women's Memorial sculpture depict?
options: Three nurses and a wounded soldier
A single nurse standing in a field
Women factory workers on a production line
questions.explain: One nurse sits on sandbags holding the wounded man, another searches the sky for a helicopter, and a third kneels holding an empty helmet.

questions.q: In what year was the Vietnam Women's Memorial dedicated?
questions.explain: The Vietnam Women's Memorial was dedicated on November 11, 1993, Veterans Day.

questions.q: What is the purpose of the In Memory plaque dedicated in 2004 near the Three Servicemen statue?
options: To list the names of Vietnam War protesters
To honor those who died later as a result of their service in Vietnam
To honor the South Vietnamese allies
To mark the end of the Paris Peace talks
questions.explain: The plaque honors men and women who died after the war as a result of their service in Vietnam.

questions.q: How high does the Vietnam Veterans Memorial wall rise at its tallest point?
questions.explain: The walls rise from 8 inches at their ends to roughly 10.1 feet at the point where they meet.

questions.q: What is The Moving Wall, first shown in Tyler, Texas, in 1984?
options: A film about the Vietnam War
A half-size traveling replica of the Wall
questions.explain: The Moving Wall is a half-size replica of the memorial. The Wall That Heals, begun in 1996, is a larger traveling replica about 375 feet long.

questions.q: What happened to the planned Vietnam Veterans Memorial Education Center in September 2018?
options: It was cancelled for lack of enough fundraising
It was converted into a library
questions.explain: The Vietnam Veterans Memorial Fund board ended the plan for the underground Education Center on September 21, 2018, after fundraising fell short, and shifted to mobile and online exhibits.

questions.q: About how many names were on the Vietnam Veterans Memorial wall when it was dedicated in 1982?
questions.explain: The Wall had 57,939 names when it was dedicated in 1982. Names have been added since, bringing the total to about 58,300.

questions.q: Which official delayed the building permit for the Vietnam Veterans Memorial amid the controversy over its design?
questions.explain: Watt delayed the building permit in 1982 until the fund agreed to add a flag and a statue to the site.

questions.q: In what year did construction of the Pentagon begin?
questions.explain: Ground was broken on September 11, 1941, and the huge building was finished in about 16 months, on January 15, 1943.

questions.q: About how long did it take to build the Pentagon?
questions.explain: Construction began September 11, 1941, and was completed January 15, 1943, during the first years of American involvement in World War II.

questions.q: How many sides does the Pentagon have?
questions.explain: The Pentagon is a five-sided building with five floors above ground and five concentric rings, lettered A to E.

questions.q: Who replaced George Bergstrom as the Pentagon's chief architect in April 1942?
questions.explain: Bergstrom was succeeded by Witmer in April 1942, while the building was being constructed wedge by wedge.

questions.q: Which Army officer pushed the Pentagon project and met the architect in July 1941, giving him days to produce a design?
questions.explain: Somervell, head of Army construction, met Bergstrom on July 17, 1941, and demanded a design for a huge office building within days.

questions.q: Which officer served as Somervell's deputy overseeing Pentagon construction before being assigned in September 1942 to run the Manhattan Project?
questions.explain: Groves oversaw day-to-day work on the Pentagon and was assigned in September 1942 to lead the secret atomic bomb program.

questions.q: Which company was the main contractor that built the Pentagon?
questions.explain: John McShain, Inc., built the Pentagon at a cost of about $83 million.

questions.q: About how much did the Pentagon cost to build?
questions.explain: The building cost roughly $83 million in 1940s dollars and was built with concrete rather than steel.

questions.q: Which river provided the sand dredged for the concrete used to build the Pentagon?
questions.explain: About 680,000 tons of sand and gravel dredged from the Potomac River were used in the concrete.

questions.q: Which neighborhood of pawnshops and homes was cleared to make room for the Pentagon?
questions.explain: Clearing the site removed Hell's Bottom, a low-lying neighborhood of pawnshops, factories and homes near Columbia Pike.

questions.q: Why did President Roosevelt move the Pentagon site away from Arlington Farms to the old Hoover Airport site?
options: To protect the view of Washington from Arlington Cemetery
To be close to the White House
Because the farm site lacked road access
To avoid flooding by the Potomac
questions.explain: The original Arlington Farms site was shifted, partly so the building would not spoil the view from Arlington National Cemetery.

questions.q: Where was the War Department housed before the Pentagon opened?
options: In temporary buildings on the National Mall and elsewhere in Washington
questions.explain: The Department of War had worked in the Munitions Building, a temporary World War I structure on the Mall, among other offices scattered around the city.

questions.q: About how many miles of corridors does the Pentagon have?
questions.explain: The Pentagon has about 17.5 miles of corridors. Its five rings and connecting hallways were designed so a person could walk between distant points fairly quickly.

questions.q: About how large is the Pentagon's floor area?
questions.explain: The Pentagon has about 6.6 million square feet of floor area, of which about 3.7 million is office space.

questions.q: The Pentagon is in which Virginia county?
questions.explain: The Pentagon stands across the Potomac from Washington, in Arlington County, Virginia.

questions.q: What nickname did the hot dog stand in the Pentagon's central courtyard receive?
questions.explain: The hot dog stand in the Pentagon's courtyard was nicknamed "Cafe Ground Zero," from a Cold War joke that Soviet planners saw the courtyard as a likely target.

questions.q: The Pentagon's Hall of Heroes honors which group?
options: Recipients of the Medal of Honor
questions.explain: The Hall of Heroes honors recipients of the Medal of Honor, with their names inscribed on the walls.

questions.q: How many people were killed at the Pentagon and on Flight 77 in the September 11 attack?
questions.explain: The 184 included 59 on the plane and 125 inside the building, not counting the hijackers.

questions.q: At what time did Flight 77 strike the Pentagon on September 11, 2001?
questions.explain: Flight 77 hit the Pentagon at 9:37 a.m., after the two attacks on the World Trade Center.

questions.q: Why was the section of the Pentagon struck on September 11, 2001, only partly occupied?
options: It was a federal holiday, so most offices were closed
A renovation was nearly done and workers were only beginning to return
An evacuation drill had just emptied most of the offices
The wedge held storage areas with very few offices
questions.explain: The section hit, Wedge 1, was almost finished with renovation and only partly reoccupied, which reduced the death toll.

questions.q: What was the Phoenix Project at the Pentagon?
options: The creation of a new cyber command
The first renovation after the building opened
The move of the Joint Chiefs to a new building
The rebuilding of the section damaged on September 11
questions.explain: The rebuilding was done quickly, and the outermost offices were reoccupied by September 11, 2002.

questions.q: How many benches are in the Pentagon Memorial?
questions.explain: The memorial has 184 illuminated benches, one engraved with the name of each victim of the attack at the Pentagon and on Flight 77.

questions.q: In what year was the Pentagon Memorial dedicated?
questions.explain: The Pentagon Memorial was dedicated on September 11, 2008, seven years after the attack.

questions.q: What lies beneath each bench of the Pentagon Memorial?
options: A shallow lighted pool of flowing water
A bronze plaque with a biography
questions.explain: Each bench has a pool of lighted flowing water beneath it, and trees shade the 1.93-acre site.

questions.q: Which two designers created the Pentagon Memorial?
options: Friedrich St. Florian and Raymond Kaskey
questions.explain: Beckman and Kaseman, with engineers Buro Happold, designed the memorial.

questions.q: The Pentagon Memorial's benches are ordered by age. What were the ages of the youngest and oldest victims?
questions.explain: The perimeter units rise from 3 inches to 71 inches to match the ages of the youngest and oldest victims.

questions.q: The Pentagon 9/11 memorial at Arlington National Cemetery is in which section?
questions.explain: The Pentagon September 11 memorial at Arlington is in Section 64. Section 60 holds service members killed since 2001.

questions.q: Which law created the National Security Council, the CIA and the Air Force as a separate branch?
questions.explain: Truman signed the National Security Act on July 26, 1947. It also set up the National Military Establishment under a secretary of defense.

questions.q: Who was the first U.S. secretary of defense?
questions.explain: Forrestal was sworn in on September 17, 1947, as head of the National Military Establishment. His powers were limited at first, until 1949 amendments converted it into an executive department, the Department of Defense, and strengthened the secretary's authority.

questions.q: What did the 1949 amendments do to the National Military Establishment?
options: Made it the cabinet-level Department of Defense
Moved it into the State Department
Abolished the Joint Chiefs of Staff
questions.explain: The amendments turned the National Military Establishment into the Department of Defense, put the services under its secretary, and gave the Joint Chiefs a full-time chairman.

questions.q: Where was the National Security Act signed by President Truman on July 26, 1947?
options: Aboard the presidential aircraft Sacred Cow
questions.explain: Truman signed the National Security Act aboard the Sacred Cow, the presidential aircraft.

questions.q: Which body of senior military officers advises the president and secretary of defense and is headquartered in the Pentagon?
questions.explain: The Joint Chiefs, established in practice in 1942 and set in law in 1947, serve as the principal military advisers.

questions.q: How many members does the Joint Chiefs of Staff have today?
questions.explain: The members are the chairman, the vice chairman, and the chiefs of the Army, Marine Corps, Navy, Air Force, Space Force and National Guard Bureau.

questions.q: Who was the first African American chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff?
questions.explain: Powell served as chairman from 1989 to 1993, including the Gulf War.

questions.q: Which 1986 law took the Joint Chiefs out of the operational chain of command?
questions.explain: Under Goldwater-Nichols, orders flow from the president through the secretary of defense to the combatant commanders.

questions.q: Which military service chief was added as a statutory member of the Joint Chiefs by the 2020 defense authorization act?
questions.explain: The 2020 NDAA made the chief of space operations a statutory member. The 2012 NDAA added the National Guard Bureau chief.

questions.q: What are the unified combatant commands of the U.S. military?
options: Joint commands of units from two or more services
Commands run by the secretary of state
questions.explain: Combatant commands combine forces from several services under one commander, and each has a geographic or functional mission.

questions.q: Which command, created in 1983, is responsible for the Middle East and is headquartered at MacDill Air Force Base in Florida?
questions.explain: CENTCOM was established on January 1, 1983, and is headquartered at MacDill Air Force Base in Florida, outside its area of responsibility.

questions.q: Which combatant command, created in 2002, is headquartered at Peterson Space Force Base in Colorado?
questions.explain: USNORTHCOM was established on October 1, 2002, in the wake of the September 11 attacks.

questions.q: Which combatant command is located at Fort George G. Meade, Maryland?
questions.explain: Cyber Command, created in 2009 as a sub-unified command under Strategic Command, was elevated to a full unified combatant command on May 4, 2018.

questions.q: Which combatant command was re-established on August 29, 2019, to focus on military operations in space?
questions.explain: The current Space Command was created in 2019. An earlier Space Command, disestablished in 2002, is considered separate.

questions.q: Where is the headquarters of U.S. European Command?
questions.explain: European Command, created in 1952, is headquartered at Patch Barracks in Stuttgart, Germany. Africa Command is also in Stuttgart.

questions.q: Which combatant command is headquartered at Camp H. M. Smith in Hawaii?
questions.explain: Indo-Pacific Command, established in 1947, is headquartered at Camp H. M. Smith, Hawaii.

questions.q: How did Congress vote on the 2001 Authorization for Use of Military Force after the September 11 attacks?
options: Both chambers by unanimous voice vote
questions.explain: Both votes were taken on September 14, 2001. Representative Barbara Lee cast the lone dissent, and Bush signed the law on September 18.

questions.q: Who cast the only vote in Congress against the 2001 Authorization for Use of Military Force?
questions.explain: Lee warned that the wording gave the president too open-ended a mandate, though she agreed that a response to the attacks was needed.

questions.q: Whose family estate became Arlington National Cemetery?
options: The family of Robert E. Lee's wife, Mary Custis Lee
The family of Ulysses S. Grant
questions.explain: The Arlington estate was built by George Washington Parke Custis. Robert E. Lee married Custis's daughter, Mary, in 1831.

questions.q: Who established the Arlington estate as a living memorial to George Washington?
questions.explain: Custis created the Arlington estate as a living memorial to George Washington.

questions.q: What was Robert E. Lee's legal relationship to the Arlington estate?
options: He managed it as executor of his father-in-law's will but never owned it
He sold it to the Army in 1861
questions.explain: Lee was executor of Custis's will and never owned the property.

questions.q: When did the U.S. Army occupy the Arlington estate during the Civil War?
questions.explain: The Army seized the estate on May 24, 1861, for its strategic position above Washington.

questions.q: Which of these was a Civil War fort built on the Arlington estate lands?
questions.explain: Forts Cass, Whipple (later Fort Myer) and McPherson were built on the estate. McPherson occupied what is now Section 11.

questions.q: What was Freedman's Village, established in June 1863 on the Arlington estate?
options: A settlement for formerly enslaved people
questions.explain: Freedman's Village occupied what are now Sections 3, 4, 8, 18 and 20 of the cemetery.

questions.q: Which cookbook author, a cousin of Custis, is the first recorded burial on the Arlington grounds?
questions.explain: Mary Randolph, who died in 1828, wrote The Virginia House-Wife and was buried on the estate decades before the cemetery existed.

questions.q: Who was the first soldier buried at Arlington National Cemetery, on May 13, 1864?
questions.explain: Christman of the 67th Pennsylvania has the oldest military grave at Arlington, buried May 13, 1864.

questions.q: On what date did Secretary of War Edwin Stanton approve Arlington as a cemetery of up to 200 acres?
questions.explain: On June 15, 1864, Meigs proposed Arlington as a national cemetery and Stanton approved the same day.

questions.q: Why did Meigs want graves placed close to the Arlington mansion?
options: To honor the officers buried in the mansion
To save money on hauling stone
To provide a view for the soldiers' families
To make the house undesirable as a residence and block the Lees from reclaiming it
questions.explain: Meigs believed burials near the house would make it unlivable and keep the Lees from returning.

questions.q: How many unknown Civil War dead were placed in the tomb that Meigs ordered built in the Arlington rose garden in 1866?
questions.explain: The tomb for unknown Civil War dead in the rose garden held 2,111 soldiers recovered near Washington.

questions.q: What did the Supreme Court decide in 1882 in the suit brought by Custis Lee over Arlington?
options: The government had taken the estate without due process
The estate remained permanently with the Lee family
The land became a national park
The Lees' suit was dismissed as too late
questions.explain: The Court ruled 5-4 for Custis Lee in 1882, finding the seizure unlawful. In 1883 he sold the property to the government for $150,000, ending the family's claim.

questions.q: Which section of Arlington was designated for African American soldiers and freed people?
questions.explain: More than 3,800 freed African Americans are buried in Section 27.

questions.q: Which section contains the Confederate graves authorized by Congress in 1900?
questions.explain: Section 16, authorized in 1900, holds the graves of 482 veterans and spouses.

questions.q: Until what year were Arlington's burial sections segregated by race, ending when Truman desegregated the military?
questions.explain: Arlington remained segregated until 1948, when President Truman desegregated the military.

questions.q: On what date was the first official Decoration Day, later Memorial Day, held at Arlington?
questions.explain: The first Decoration Day ceremony was held at Arlington on May 30, 1868.

questions.q: After which war did the government begin repatriating war dead at its own expense, adding Arlington Sections 21, 22 and 24?
questions.explain: In 1899 the government began repatriating war dead from the Spanish-American War, and the cemetery expanded.

questions.q: In which sections were more than 2,000 repatriated World War I dead buried at Arlington?
questions.explain: More than 2,000 service members returned after World War I were interred in Sections 18 and 19.

questions.q: About how many people are buried at Arlington National Cemetery today?
questions.explain: Arlington holds nearly 430,000 veterans and eligible family members, with about 27 to 30 funerals per day.

questions.q: About how many acres does Arlington National Cemetery cover today?
questions.explain: The original cemetery covered 200 acres. It has grown to 639 acres.

questions.q: Which section of Arlington is the burial ground for service members killed in the post-2001 conflicts?
questions.explain: Section 60 is the burial ground for those killed in the war on terror since 2001.

questions.q: What is the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier at Arlington?
options: A memorial to the Revolutionary War
A marble tomb marking the graves of unidentified American service members
A tower honoring Civil War generals
questions.explain: The Tomb began with an unidentified World War I soldier interred on November 11, 1921, and now honors unknowns from several wars.

questions.q: On what date was the World War I Unknown interred at Arlington?
questions.explain: The World War I Unknown was selected at Chalons-sur-Marne, France, and interred on November 11, 1921.

questions.q: In which French city was the World War I Unknown Soldier selected before coming to Arlington?
questions.explain: The unknown was selected at Chalons-sur-Marne and interred at Arlington on November 11, 1921.

questions.q: Which president placed the Medal of Honor on the World War I Unknown's casket in 1921?
questions.explain: Harding placed the Medal of Honor on the casket at the November 11, 1921, ceremony.

questions.q: Which three figures decorate the front of the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier's sarcophagus, completed in 1932?
questions.explain: Three figures on the front represent Peace, Victory and Valor.

questions.q: What does the inscription on the back of the sarcophagus of the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier at Arlington National Cemetery say?
options: Here rests in honored glory an American soldier known but to God
Here lies a soldier whose name is lost to history
To our fallen sons, forever remembered
They gave their last full measure of devotion
questions.explain: The inscription reads, "Here rests in honored glory an American soldier known but to God."

questions.q: When did Fort Myer soldiers begin guarding the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier, at first only in daylight?
questions.explain: Fort Myer soldiers first guarded the Tomb in 1926, in daylight only. Guarding became around the clock in 1937.

questions.q: In what year did guarding of the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier become a 24-hour duty?
questions.explain: The Army ordered around-the-clock guarding at the Tomb in 1937, and it has continued since.

questions.q: Which Army unit has guarded the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier since 1948?
options: The 3rd U.S. Infantry Regiment (The Old Guard)
questions.explain: The 3rd U.S. Infantry Regiment, known as The Old Guard, has guarded the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier since April 6, 1948. Sentinels keep watch around the clock.

questions.q: What does the number 21 in the routine of the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier's sentinels recall?
options: The number of wars the nation has fought
The age of the first unknown
The number of presidents buried at Arlington
questions.explain: The routine of 21 steps and 21-second pauses honors the 21-gun salute, the highest military honor.

questions.q: Which wars' unknown service members were interred at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier in 1958?
options: The Spanish-American War and World War I
The Civil War and World War I
Korean War and the Vietnam War
World War II and the Korean War
questions.explain: Unknowns from World War II and the Korean War were interred together at Arlington on May 30, 1958.

questions.q: Who was the Vietnam War Unknown whose remains were identified by DNA testing in 1998?
options: Air Force 1st Lt. Michael J. Blassie
questions.explain: The Vietnam Unknown was interred at the Tomb in 1984. After DNA testing identified him in 1998, he was reinterred in St. Louis.

questions.q: What became of the Vietnam Unknown's crypt after the remains were identified in 1998?
options: It was rededicated to all missing Vietnam service members
It received a second Vietnam unknown
It was moved to the Capitol
questions.explain: The crypt was rededicated in 1999 to all missing Vietnam service members.

questions.q: Which president, buried at Arlington in 1930, was the first of only two presidents interred there?
questions.explain: Taft was buried at Arlington in 1930. John F. Kennedy became the second president there on November 25, 1963.

questions.q: Who lit the eternal flame at President Kennedy's grave at the end of the burial service?
questions.explain: Jacqueline Kennedy lit the flame at the end of the burial service on November 25, 1963. It was moved to the permanent Eternal Flame in March 1967.

questions.q: How was the temporary flame at Kennedy's grave built for the November 1963 funeral?
options: A natural gas line from the Capitol was extended
Army engineers improvised it from a modified propane torch
Candles were placed in a glass cup
A torch from the Olympic Games was relit
questions.explain: Col. Clayton B. Lyle and an Army Corps of Engineers team improvised a temporary flame from a modified propane tiki torch.

questions.q: Which architect designed Kennedy's permanent grave, opened to the public on March 15, 1967?
questions.explain: Warnecke, a longtime friend of Kennedy, designed the permanent gravesite with an elliptical plaza and terrace.

questions.q: Which Kennedy family member, buried at Arlington in June 1968, was moved to a permanent gravesite there in December 1971?
questions.explain: Robert F. Kennedy, assassinated in June 1968, was buried at Arlington on June 8, 1968, and moved to a permanent gravesite on December 1, 1971.

questions.q: Which commander of the Tuskegee Airmen and first Black Air Force brigadier general is buried at Arlington?
questions.explain: Davis commanded the Tuskegee Airmen in World War II and became the first Black brigadier general in the Air Force.

questions.q: Which first American to orbit Earth was buried at Arlington in April 2017?
questions.explain: Glenn, also a longtime Ohio senator, was buried at Arlington in April 2017.

questions.q: Which Apollo 1 astronauts, killed in a January 27, 1967, flash fire, are buried at Arlington?
questions.explain: Grissom and Chaffee died on the launch pad on January 27, 1967, and both rest at Arlington.

questions.q: Which two Challenger shuttle crew members have individual graves at Arlington National Cemetery?
options: Commander Dick Scobee and pilot Michael J. Smith
questions.explain: Challenger broke apart 73 seconds after liftoff on January 28, 1986. Scobee and Smith are buried at Arlington.

questions.q: What technical failure caused the Challenger disaster, according to the Rogers Commission?
options: An engine fire in the orbiter
A collision with a bird at launch
A computer fault in the guidance system
The failure of O-ring seals on a solid rocket booster in cold weather
questions.explain: Cold temperatures stiffened the rubber O-rings, and hot gas burned through. Richard Feynman demonstrated the effect in a hearing.

questions.q: Which Army Chinook pilot and company commander, killed in a crash on March 1, 1991, just after the Gulf War cease-fire, is buried at Arlington?
questions.explain: Maj. Marie Rossi, who commanded a Chinook company in the Gulf War, died when her helicopter struck a tower on March 1, 1991.

questions.q: According to the cemetery, about how many Medal of Honor recipients are buried or memorialized at Arlington?
questions.explain: Arlington says more than 400 Medal of Honor recipients are buried or memorialized there, from the Civil War to current conflicts.

questions.q: Why is Richard McKinley, who died in the 1961 SL-1 reactor explosion, buried in a lead-lined casket at Arlington?
options: He was buried at sea first
His family requested it for security
He died of an infectious disease
questions.explain: McKinley died in the 1961 SL-1 reactor explosion, and his remains are so radioactive that he is in a lead-lined casket.

questions.q: Which Arlington memorial honors the U.S. Navy warship lost in Havana harbor in 1898?
questions.explain: The mast of the USS Maine stands at Arlington. The Lockerbie Cairn honors victims of the 1988 Pan Am Flight 103 bombing.

questions.q: What tradition takes place at gravestones at Arlington before each Memorial Day?
options: A cannon is fired at each grave
Candles are lit at each gravestone
Wreaths are laid by the president at every grave
Flags are placed at each grave
questions.explain: Soldiers of the 3d U.S. Infantry (The Old Guard) place small flags at every gravestone on the Thursday before Memorial Day.

questions.q: Which French admiral's fleet cut off Cornwallis from the sea at the Battle of the Chesapeake on September 5, 1781?
questions.explain: De Grasse defeated a British fleet, cutting off Cornwallis from reinforcement or escape by sea.

questions.q: Who surrendered the British army at Yorktown in place of the ailing Cornwallis on October 19, 1781?
questions.explain: Cornwallis skipped the ceremony, citing illness. O'Hara surrendered, and Washington denied the British the traditional honors of war.

questions.q: About how many British and allied soldiers were captured at Yorktown?
questions.explain: About 8,000 British and allied soldiers were captured at Yorktown, ending the last major land campaign of the Revolution.

questions.q: Which battle on August 24, 1814, opened the road for the British to enter Washington?
questions.explain: After defeating American troops at Bladensburg, the British entered Washington and burned the White House and Capitol; retreating Americans had already burned the Navy Yard.

questions.q: How did the burning of Washington end?
options: The British were driven out by a Virginia militia counterattack
Dolley Madison negotiated a truce with Admiral Cockburn
Congress paid a ransom to the British commanders
A thunderstorm helped put out the fires and the British left after about 26 hours
questions.explain: A violent thunderstorm put out the fires. The British occupation lasted about 26 hours.

questions.q: Who is famous for helping save a copy of the Gilbert Stuart portrait of Washington from the White House in 1814?
questions.explain: Dolley Madison oversaw the removal of valuables, including the Stuart portrait of Washington. Staff members, among them doorkeeper Jean Pierre Sioussat and the gardener, took it down.

questions.q: Where did Congress meet after the Capitol was burned in 1814?
options: The Post and Patent Office building, then the Old Brick Capitol
The Senate wing of the Treasury
questions.explain: Congress met in the Patent Office, then in the Old Brick Capitol in 1815, while the burned Capitol was rebuilt over several years.

questions.q: How much did the United States pay Mexico under the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo?
questions.explain: Mexico ceded California, New Mexico and much of the Southwest for $15 million.

questions.q: Which U.S. president led the country into the Mexican-American War?
questions.explain: Polk was president throughout the war, with Zachary Taylor and Winfield Scott leading U.S. forces.

questions.q: Which two generals led the main U.S. armies in the Mexican-American War?
options: Stonewall Jackson and Robert E. Lee
questions.explain: Taylor led forces in northern Mexico and Scott led the campaign toward Mexico City.

questions.q: Which present-day states were part of the Mexican Cession?
options: California, Nevada, Utah, Arizona and New Mexico, plus parts of other states
questions.explain: Mexico ceded present-day California, Nevada, Utah, New Mexico and Arizona, plus parts of Colorado, Oklahoma, Kansas and Wyoming.

questions.q: On what date did the United States declare war on Germany in World War I?
questions.explain: Wilson asked Congress for war on April 2, 1917. Congress approved on April 6.

questions.q: What was the Zimmermann Telegram?
options: A British warning about German spies
A German proposal for an alliance with Mexico against the United States
A French request for U.S. troops
questions.explain: German Foreign Minister Arthur Zimmermann sent it on January 16, 1917, and its disclosure helped push the United States toward war.

questions.q: Which ocean liner sunk by a German submarine on May 7, 1915, killed 128 Americans?
questions.explain: The Lusitania sinking killed nearly 1,200 people, including 128 Americans, and turned many Americans against Germany.

questions.q: Who commanded the American Expeditionary Forces in World War I?
questions.explain: Pershing commanded U.S. forces on the Western Front. He was later given a state funeral and buried at Arlington.

questions.q: What did Germany announce on January 31, 1917, that helped lead to American entry into World War I?
options: A naval blockade of Britain by surface ships only
questions.explain: Germany announced on January 31, 1917, that unrestricted submarine warfare would resume on February 1, putting American ships at risk.

questions.q: What do the 56 pillars of the National WWII Memorial represent?
options: The 56 battles of the American war effort
The states, the District of Columbia and territories that took part in the war
questions.explain: The pillars stand for the 48 states, the District of Columbia and the U.S. territories of the war years, 56 in all.

questions.q: What links the granite pillars at the National WWII Memorial together?
options: A bronze rope symbolizing national unity
questions.explain: The bronze rope symbolizes unity against tyranny among the states and territories.

questions.q: What two bronze wreaths appear on each pillar at the National WWII Memorial?
options: Laurel for victory and olive for peace
Pine for the Navy and palm for the Army
Wheat for agriculture and oak for industry
Cotton for the South and corn for the West
questions.explain: The wreaths honor farm and factory production at home during the war.

questions.q: How many gold stars are on the Freedom Wall at the National WWII Memorial?
questions.explain: Each of the 4,048 gold stars represents 100 American lives lost in the war.

questions.q: What does each gold star on the Freedom Wall represent?
options: One state that took part in the war
One major battle of the war
100 American lives lost in the war
questions.explain: Together the stars stand for more than 400,000 Americans who died in World War II.

questions.q: What is inscribed on the Freedom Wall at the National WWII Memorial?
options: Here We Mark The Price Of Freedom
The Only Thing We Have To Fear Is Fear Itself
questions.explain: The wall on the west side of the memorial carries that inscription above the field of gold stars.

questions.q: Which two pavilions mark the north and south ends of the National WWII Memorial?
questions.explain: The 43-foot Atlantic and Pacific Pavilions honor the war's two main theaters.

questions.q: How many bronze eagles hold a laurel wreath in each pavilion of the National WWII Memorial?
questions.explain: Each pavilion has four bronze eagles holding a laurel wreath, a classical symbol of victory.

questions.q: Which inscriptions appear on the floors of the World War II Memorial's pavilions?
options: Victory on Land, Victory at Sea and Victory in the Air
questions.explain: Each pavilion floor shows the World War II Victory Medal and inscriptions for victory on land, at sea and in the air.

questions.q: Who sculpted the 24 bronze bas-relief panels at the National WWII Memorial?
questions.explain: Raymond Kaskey sculpted the memorial's 24 bronze bas-relief panels, which show Americans at war overseas and on the home front.

questions.q: In what year was the National WWII Memorial dedicated?
questions.explain: The National World War II Memorial was dedicated on May 29, 2004, during Memorial Day weekend. It stands on the National Mall between the Washington Monument and Lincoln Memorial.

questions.q: Who was the architect of the National WWII Memorial?
questions.explain: St. Florian's design was selected in 1997. It combines classical architecture with layered symbolism.

questions.q: What historic feature stands at the center of the National WWII Memorial plaza?
questions.explain: The memorial replaced and restored the Rainbow Pool at the eastern end of the Reflecting Pool.

questions.q: Between which two landmarks does the National WWII Memorial sit along the Mall's east-west axis?
options: The Capitol and the Washington Monument
The Washington Monument and the Lincoln Memorial
The Jefferson Memorial and the White House
The Lincoln Memorial and the Pentagon
questions.explain: The memorial lies between the Washington Monument and the Lincoln Memorial in the heart of the National Mall.

questions.q: About how many Americans served in the military during World War II, according to the National Park Service?
questions.explain: The memorial honors 16 million who served, millions more on the home front, and more than 400,000 who died.

questions.q: Which 1993 law, signed by President Clinton, authorized the National WWII Memorial?
options: The World War II Memorial Act (Public Law 103-32)
questions.explain: Clinton signed the World War II Memorial Act on May 25, 1993.

questions.q: Which World War II veteran's question to Representative Marcy Kaptur at a fish fry led her to introduce a memorial bill in 1987?
questions.explain: Durbin approached Kaptur of Ohio, who introduced a bill for the memorial in 1987 and reintroduced it in later sessions.

questions.q: Who co-chaired the corporate fundraising effort for the National WWII Memorial with Frederick W. Smith?
questions.explain: Dole co-chaired the national campaign with Frederick W. Smith. It raised about $197 million in cash and pledges, including about $16 million in federal funds.

questions.q: About how much money was raised to build the National WWII Memorial?
questions.explain: The campaign raised about $197 million in cash and pledges, including about $16 million in federal funds.

questions.q: What was the main objection raised by opponents of the World War II Memorial's site on the Mall?
options: It was too far from the Capitol
It would damage the cherry trees
It was too close to Arlington Cemetery
It interrupted the view between the Washington Monument and the Lincoln Memorial
questions.explain: The National Coalition to Save Our Mall opposed the location, mainly for interrupting the view down the Mall.

questions.q: What informal graffiti-style engraving appears twice in the National WWII Memorial?
questions.explain: Two inconspicuous "Kilroy was here" engravings were included as a nod to the soldiers' wartime joke.

questions.q: When was ground broken for the National WWII Memorial?
questions.explain: Ground was broken in November 2000, and the memorial was dedicated in May 2004.

questions.q: How many Americans were killed in the attack on Pearl Harbor?
questions.explain: The attack killed 2,403 military and civilians and wounded 1,178.

questions.q: How did Roosevelt describe December 7, 1941, in his address to Congress?
options: A date which will live in infamy
The dawn of a new war
questions.explain: Roosevelt asked Congress to declare war on Japan on December 8.

questions.q: Which U.S. ships were not in port during the Pearl Harbor attack and escaped damage?
questions.explain: The carriers Enterprise and Lexington were at sea and Saratoga was on the West Coast, so none was at Pearl Harbor.

questions.q: About how many Japanese aircraft took part in the two waves of the Pearl Harbor attack?
questions.explain: Japan launched about 353 aircraft in two waves from six aircraft carriers on December 7, 1941. The attack sank or damaged many ships of the Pacific Fleet.

questions.q: Which Japanese admiral planned the attack on Pearl Harbor?
questions.explain: Yamamoto planned the attack, and Nagumo commanded the strike force.

questions.q: Which countries declared war on the United States on December 11, 1941?
questions.explain: Germany and Italy declared war on the United States on December 11, 1941, after the U.S. declared war on Japan.

questions.q: What was the code name of the Allied invasion of Normandy?
questions.explain: The amphibious phase, Operation Neptune, began on June 6, 1944, as part of Overlord.

questions.q: On what date did the D-Day landings in Normandy take place?
questions.explain: The Allied landings began shortly after midnight with airborne drops, then amphibious landings at about 6:30 a.m. on June 6.

questions.q: Which general commanded the Allied forces for the Normandy invasion?
questions.explain: Eisenhower commanded Allied forces (SHAEF). Erwin Rommel commanded German defenses.

questions.q: Which beach had the highest number of Allied casualties on D-Day?
questions.explain: Omaha, a sector with high cliffs, had the highest number of casualties.

questions.q: How many beach sectors were used in the Normandy landings?
questions.explain: The June 6, 1944, Normandy landings used five beach sectors: Utah and Omaha for American troops, Gold and Sword for British troops, and Juno for Canadian troops.

questions.q: Which two U.S. airborne divisions landed behind Utah Beach on D-Day?
questions.explain: The 82nd and 101st Airborne landed west of Utah Beach in the early hours of June 6.

questions.q: Why was D-Day postponed by one day from June 5 to June 6, 1944?
options: Because of a German peace offer
Because ships were delayed in the Atlantic
Because of high winds, heavy seas and low cloud
questions.explain: Eisenhower chose June 6 after meteorologist James Stagg predicted improvement.

questions.q: What was the Battle of the Bulge?
options: A German counteroffensive in the Ardennes in December 1944
A naval battle in the Pacific
questions.explain: It began December 16, 1944, and was the largest and bloodiest single battle fought by the United States in the war.

questions.q: What did Hitler hope to capture in the Battle of the Bulge?
questions.explain: Hitler aimed to split the Allied lines and seize Antwerp, but the offensive failed.

questions.q: Which American admiral led the U.S. Pacific Fleet at the Battle of Midway?
questions.explain: Nimitz commanded the Pacific Fleet. Spruance took over the carrier task force during the battle.

questions.q: Which U.S. Navy codebreaking unit, led by Joseph Rochefort, learned the Japanese plan for Midway?
questions.explain: Station HYPO's codebreakers learned the date and place of the attack, so Nimitz could set an ambush.

questions.q: What was the first atomic test, conducted in New Mexico on July 16, 1945, called?
questions.explain: The Trinity test exceeded expectations and was followed by the bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki.

questions.q: Which two Japanese cities were hit by atomic bombs in August 1945?
questions.explain: A uranium bomb was dropped on Hiroshima on August 6 and a plutonium bomb on Nagasaki on August 9, 1945.

questions.q: Who headed the Los Alamos laboratory where the atomic bombs were designed?
questions.explain: Oppenheimer organized and headed Los Alamos. Groves directed the overall Manhattan Project.

questions.q: Which declaration of July 26, 1945, demanded Japan's unconditional surrender?
questions.explain: The Potsdam Declaration threatened prompt and utter destruction. The Japanese government ignored it.

questions.q: On what date did Japan sign the instrument of surrender ending World War II?
questions.explain: Japan announced its surrender on August 15 and signed the surrender instrument on September 2.

questions.q: Which Army colonel commanded the 509th Composite Group that carried out the atomic bombings?
questions.explain: Tibbets commanded the group, which trained for and carried out the missions.

questions.q: About how much aid did Congress approve for Greece and Turkey in May 1947 under the Truman Doctrine?
questions.explain: Congress approved about $400 million in military and economic aid, of which Turkey received $100 million.

questions.q: Which diplomat's 1946 "Long Telegram" laid out the idea of containing Soviet expansion?
questions.explain: Kennan's Long Telegram proposed the containment strategy behind the Truman Doctrine.

questions.q: Which journalist criticized the Truman Doctrine's pledge as open-ended?
questions.explain: Walter Lippmann was among critics who saw the pledge as too open-ended.

questions.q: What was the Berlin Airlift?
options: Allied supply of West Berlin by air during a Soviet blockade
A rescue of American prisoners from Korea
A bombing campaign against East Germany
A transport of troops to Vietnam
questions.explain: The Soviets blocked road, rail and canal access to West Berlin from June 24, 1948. The Allies flew in supplies until the blockade ended.

questions.q: On what date did the Soviet blockade of West Berlin begin?
questions.explain: The blockade began on June 24, 1948, and the airlift started two days later.

questions.q: What was the American name for the Berlin Airlift?
questions.explain: The U.S. called it Operation Vittles and the British called it Operation Plainfare.

questions.q: What event triggered the Soviet blockade of West Berlin?
options: The introduction of the Deutsche Mark in the Western zones
The founding of the Warsaw Pact
The construction of the Berlin Wall
questions.explain: The Western Allies announced a currency reform and the Deutsche Mark was introduced in West Berlin. The Soviets rejected it and imposed the blockade.

questions.q: Which U.S. general ordered the Berlin Airlift to begin?
questions.explain: General Clay ordered the airlift to start, and William H. Tunner later reorganized it.

questions.q: Which Air Force general reorganized the Berlin Airlift's flight operations in the summer of 1948?
questions.explain: Tunner took charge of the airlift in late July 1948. After the accidents of August 13, 1948, he imposed stricter procedures that made it succeed.

questions.q: About how many tons of supplies did Western aircraft deliver to Berlin during the airlift?
questions.explain: Western aircraft made 278,228 flights and delivered 2,334,374 tons, nearly two-thirds of it coal.

questions.q: On what date did the Soviets lift the Berlin blockade?
questions.explain: The blockade ended on May 12, 1949, but the airlift continued until September 30.

questions.q: Which new Berlin airport was built by the French during the airlift?
questions.explain: Tempelhof and Gatow were used from the start, and the French built Tegel.

questions.q: Which 1962 confrontation brought the United States and Soviet Union close to nuclear war over missiles in Cuba?
questions.explain: The crisis lasted from October 16 to 28, 1962, after a U-2 photographed Soviet missile sites in Cuba.

questions.q: What did Kennedy call the naval blockade he ordered around Cuba on October 22, 1962?
questions.explain: He used the word quarantine to avoid the formal implications of a declaration of war.

questions.q: Who presented the evidence of Soviet missiles in Cuba to the UN Security Council?
questions.explain: U.S. Ambassador Adlai Stevenson presented the evidence to the Security Council.

questions.q: What was agreed publicly to end the Cuban Missile Crisis?
options: The Soviets would dismantle missiles in Cuba, and the U.S. pledged not to invade
The U.S. would pay Cuba reparations
The U.S. would leave Guantanamo Bay
questions.explain: The U.S. also secretly agreed to remove Jupiter missiles from Turkey.

questions.q: What was the Moscow-Washington hotline, created after the Cuban Missile Crisis?
options: A direct communication link between the two leaders
questions.explain: The crisis led to the hotline so the leaders could communicate directly.

questions.q: Which U-2 pilot was killed during the Cuban Missile Crisis?
questions.explain: A U.S. U-2 was lost over Cuba, and its pilot, Rudolf Anderson, was killed.

questions.q: What event in August 1990 began the Gulf War crisis?
questions.explain: Iraq invaded Kuwait on August 2, 1990, and a U.S.-led coalition built up forces in Operation Desert Shield.

questions.q: What were the two U.S. operation names for the 1990-1991 Gulf War buildup and combat?
questions.explain: Desert Shield covered the buildup, and Desert Storm ran from January 17 to February 28, 1991.

questions.q: On what date did the Gulf War air campaign begin?
questions.explain: The coalition began its air and naval bombardment on January 17 and continued about five weeks.

questions.q: What deadline did UN Security Council Resolution 678 set for Iraq to leave Kuwait?
questions.explain: The resolution authorized all necessary means if Iraq had not left by January 15, 1991.

questions.q: When did the coalition ground offensive begin in the Gulf War?
questions.explain: The ground offensive began on February 24 and a ceasefire followed within 100 hours.

questions.q: About how many countries joined the U.S.-led coalition against Iraq in the Gulf War?
questions.explain: More than 30 countries joined the U.S.-led coalition, a very broad military alliance. Counts range from about 35 to 42 depending on how members are counted.

questions.q: Who was the U.S. president during the Gulf War?
questions.explain: George H. W. Bush led the U.S. side, and General Norman Schwarzkopf commanded coalition forces.

questions.q: Which general led U.S. Central Command and the U.S.-led coalition's forces in the Gulf War?
questions.explain: Schwarzkopf led U.S. Central Command and the coalition's forces in the Gulf War. Colin Powell was chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff.

questions.q: Which military operation began in October 2001 after the September 11 attacks?
questions.explain: The war began on October 7, 2001, and ended with the U.S. withdrawal in late August 2021.

questions.q: Which NATO-led force, authorized in December 2001, supported Afghanistan's government until 2014?
options: ISAF, the International Security Assistance Force
questions.explain: ISAF was authorized by the UN in December 2001 and led by NATO from 2003 until 2014, followed by the Resolute Support mission from 2015 to 2021.

questions.q: Where was Osama bin Laden killed in a May 2011 raid by Navy SEALs?
questions.explain: The raid took place on the night of May 1-2, 2011, in Abbottabad.

questions.q: What was the code name of the 2011 raid that killed Osama bin Laden?
questions.explain: About two dozen Navy SEALs flew in on helicopters, and bin Laden was buried at sea.

questions.q: When did the Iraq War begin with the U.S.-led invasion?
